screens.title: Architecting for Governance and Compliance
screens.narratorSegment: In large cloud estates, governance is not optional — it is the architecture that keeps your environment secure, auditable, and predictable. In this lesson you will learn how AWS Organizations provides the account hierarchy you need, how Service Control Policies act as preventive guardrails, and how AWS Config and CloudTrail become your continuous detective controls. You will see a concrete remediation pattern where Config rules detect a misconfigured S3 bucket and a Lambda function automatically restores encryption. Understanding the shared responsibility model is essential: AWS secures the underlying infrastructure while you must design, configure, and operate your workloads to meet compliance frameworks such as PCI, HIPAA, GDPR, and ISO 27001. Along the way we’ll point out common mistakes, like trying to use SCPs to grant permissions, or storing logs without protecting them from deletion. By the end of this chapter you’ll be able to propose a multi-account structure with OUs and SCPs, define Config rules for continuous evaluation, plan an automated remediation workflow, and explain who is responsible for each control during an audit. Consider what compliance requirement is most critical for your organization and how a combination of preventative guardrails and automated remediation would reduce manual work and risk.

screens.title: The architect’s governance responsibilities
screens.narratorSegment: As a solutions architect, your responsibilities stretch beyond selecting services and writing CloudFormation. Governance is the set of patterns you design so the organization can operate securely and consistently across many accounts. That includes designing an account structure, deciding which actions are allowed or denied, choosing how logs are collected, and defining automated responses to non-compliant states. A concrete example is when an enterprise has separate accounts for finance, dev, and production: you would use Organizational Units to group accounts and apply policies tailored to risk — for instance, stricter restrictions for finance. A common misconception is that governance is only about blocking actions; in reality it balances prevention, detection, and remediation. Prevention reduces risk, but detective controls like AWS Config and CloudTrail provide evidence and help you discover gaps. For architects, the practical significance is twofold: first, policies reduce human error and accidental exposure; second, a clear governance design produces audit evidence that simplifies compliance reporting. When you design governance, think in patterns: where should a preventive guardrail be applied, what should be monitored, and what should be fixed automatically? This framing helps you justify architecture decisions to stakeholders and prepares you for audits. What part of your current account strategy would you formalize into an OU today?

keyIdea.title: Governance Responsibility
keyIdea.text: Design policies for prevention, detection, and remediation across accounts; balance operational needs with strict controls for sensitive units.

content.html:
Core Concept
The architect’s governance responsibilities
Governance includes account design, guardrails, monitoring, and automated remediation to enforce policy at scale.
Definition
Governance is the set of policies and operational patterns that ensure security, compliance, and consistency across multiple AWS accounts.
Concrete example
Group finance accounts into an OU, attach stricter SCPs to deny unapproved regions and services, and collect logs centrally for auditors.
Common misconception
Governance is not only blocking: you also need detective controls and remediation to operate safely and show evidence to auditors.
Key Takeaway

Design governance as prevention, detection, and remediation. Use OUs to mirror risk boundaries and ensure evidence collection for audits.

Analogy & scenario
Analogy
Think of governance as traffic rules: guardrails (SCPs) set where you cannot drive, signs (Config + CloudTrail) record infractions, and patrols (Lambda) correct dangerous behavior automatically.
Scenario
A developer accidentally creates an unencrypted storage bucket in a dev account. With governance in place, Config flags the bucket and a remediation Lambda applies default encryption, preventing data exposure.
Check your understanding
When would you choose a preventive SCP versus a detective Config rule? Consider the impact on developer productivity and audit evidence needs.

screens.title: AWS Organizations and Organizational Units
screens.narratorSegment: AWS Organizations is the foundation for multi-account governance: it lets you consolidate accounts, centralize billing, and apply policies to groups of accounts. Organizational Units let you mirror organizational structure — for example, create OUs for engineering, finance, and production. Applying policies at the OU level is powerful because it avoids per-account replication and reduces configuration drift. A concrete example is attaching an SCP to an OU that denies launching instances in disallowed regions. Remember that SCPs define the maximum available permissions; they do not grant access. A frequent mistake is relying solely on an OU without thinking through exceptions — some accounts may require special allowances. To test safely, create a sandbox OU and a test account before applying broad SCPs. Operationally, you should also plan a logging account where CloudTrail and aggregated logs are stored, and a security account for centralized alerting. The practical insight for architects is to design OUs and SCPs so they enforce business rules while minimizing legitimate operational friction. How would you represent your organization in OUs to simplify policy application? AWS Organizations and Organizational Units means use organizations and ous to group accounts, apply policies at scale, and centralize billing and logging for consistent governance and auditability.. In practical terms, structure accounts so policies and billing are manageable at scale. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Use Organizations and OUs to group accounts, apply policies at scale, and centralize billing and logging for consistent governance and auditability.

content.html:
Process Flow
AWS Organizations & OUs
Group accounts into OUs that map to business units or risk profiles, and apply policies at the OU level.
Step 1: Create Organization
Establish a management account and enable AWS Organizations to centrally manage accounts and billing.
Step 2: Create OUs
Group accounts into logical units such as dev, prod, and security for targeted policy application.
Step 3: Plan Logging and Security Accounts
Designate accounts for centralized CloudTrail logs and security tooling to protect logs from tampering.
Pro tip

Model OUs to minimize exceptions. Use a sandbox OU to validate SCPs before applying them broadly.

Reference architecture
Example OU layout
  • Root
  • ├─ Security (logging, SIEM)
  • ├─ Production (strict SCPs)
  • └─ Development (fewer restrictions)
Example policy use
Attach an SCP to Production OU that denies creating resources in disallowed regions and deleting centralized logs.
Check your understanding
Why is it safer to test SCPs in a sandbox OU before applying to production? Think about accidental denial of critical actions.

screens.title: Service Control Policies (SCPs)
screens.narratorSegment: Service Control Policies are a central mechanism to set preventive guardrails across accounts. An SCP filters the maximum permissions an account or OU can exercise; it does not grant permissions by itself. For example, an SCP attached to an OU could deny the ability to create resources in a specific region or denying deletion of audit trails. A practical contrast helps: IAM policies grant or deny for a specific user or role, whereas SCPs restrict everything in an account regardless of those IAM policies, subject to the effective permission intersection. A common mistake is attempting to use an SCP as an IAM policy — because SCPs cannot grant access, an overly restrictive SCP can accidentally block administrators. To avoid that, test policies in a sandbox and use Allow-lists carefully. Another misconception is that SCPs replace logging or remediation: they prevent many misconfigurations, but you still need detective controls like Config and CloudTrail to record what did happen. The key outcome is this: use SCPs to enforce enterprise policy boundaries and prevent entire classes of risky actions, while leaving day-to-day access control to IAM within those bounds. How would you craft an SCP to prevent data storage in a disallowed region while permitting normal operations elsewhere?

keyIdea.title: SCP Essentials
keyIdea.text: SCPs set the maximum permissions across accounts or OUs. They are preventative and cannot grant permissions. Test them to avoid accidental lockouts.

content.html:
Definition
Service Control Policies
SCPs centrally limit the maximum permissions for accounts and OUs. They prevent actions before they occur.
Claim
An SCP defines what is allowed at most for an account or OU. It cannot grant additional permissions.
Concrete example
Attach an SCP to an OU that denies creating buckets in eu-west-2 to enforce data residency rules for all accounts in that OU.
Misuse to avoid
Do not rely on SCPs to grant access. Avoid overly broad denies that block legitimate administrative tasks; always validate in a sandbox.
Key Takeaway

Use SCPs as preventive guardrails and test them thoroughly. They shape the maximum permissions available across accounts.

Comparison: SCPs vs IAM
SCP
Prevents actions at the account or OU level. Does not grant permissions.
IAM Policy
Grants or denies permissions to identities. Effective permissions are intersection of IAM and SCP boundaries.
Design question
Which operations should be prevented organization-wide and which should be controlled per-role? Use that to split SCPs and IAM policies.

screens.title: Common SCP pitfalls and safe testing patterns
screens.narratorSegment: SCPs are powerful, and power invites mistakes if you move too quickly. A frequent pitfall is creating a deny that inadvertently prevents critical management actions, such as updating CloudTrail configurations or applying patching tasks. Another mistake is assuming that an SCP will provide audit logs — SCPs prevent actions; they do not record them. To mitigate risk, adopt a safe testing pattern: first apply the SCP to a sandbox OU or a single test account, then simulate common administrative workflows to ensure no legitimate tasks are blocked. Use explicit denies sparingly and prefer targeted statements that address a specific risk, such as denying resource creation in a banned region. Also plan exception processes for accounts that must break the pattern, documented and approved. A practical test you can run is attempting to create a resource that the SCP would deny and confirming the expected failure message, then checking CloudTrail to confirm the attempted A P I call was recorded. The final takeaway is to treat SCP changes like schema changes: version them, review them, and deploy them progressively. What verification steps would you add to your change process to ensure an SCP doesn't block an essential operation?

keyIdea.title: Safe SCP Practices
keyIdea.text: Test SCPs in a sandbox, prefer narrow denies, version and review policies, and validate administrative workflows before broad rollout.

content.html:
Comparison
SCP pitfalls & safe testing
Avoid overly broad denies and validate SCPs in a sandbox before production deployment.
Pitfall: Over-blocking
An SCP can block legitimate admin tasks. Test common workflows before applying to production OUs.
Pitfall: Expecting logging
SCPs do not produce audit logs of attempted denies; rely on CloudTrail for recording API calls and attempted actions.
Safe pattern
Version SCPs, test in a sandbox OU, simulate admin workflows, and roll out progressively with rollback plans.
Check

Before applying an SCP broadly, try to perform essential admin tasks in a test account to confirm no disruption.

Validation checklist
Define the SCP change and its purpose clearly.
Apply to sandbox OU and run admin scenario tests.
Review CloudTrail for attempted calls and confirm expected rejections.
Plan rollback steps and approval gate for production deployment.

screens.title: AWS Config and Config Rules
screens.narratorSegment: AWS Config provides a continuous inventory of your resource configurations and records changes over time. It lets you define Config Rules that evaluate whether resources meet your desired conditions — for example, requiring S3 buckets to have default encryption or ensuring EC2 instances have specific tags. When a rule marks a resource NON_COMPLIANT, Config can emit notifications and trigger remediation workflows. A concrete example is the S3 default encryption rule: when an unencrypted bucket is detected, Config can publish an evaluation event that invokes a Lambda function to apply server-side encryption and return the resource to compliance. A common misconception is that Config replaces auditing practices; instead, it complements them. Config gives you continuous evaluation and point-in-time configuration history, while CloudTrail records who made A P I calls. For architects, the design decision is which rules to enforce automatically and which to surface for manual review. Automating low-risk fixes like enabling encryption reduces toil, while higher-risk changes may require human approval. When building rules, consider evaluation frequency, scope, and whether remediation should be manual or automatic. Which resource types in your environment would you automate and which would you review manually?

keyIdea.title: Config Fundamentals
keyIdea.text: AWS Config records resource state and evaluates rules; use it to detect drift and trigger remediation workflows for non-compliant resources.

content.html:
Core Concept
AWS Config & Rules
Continuously evaluate resource configurations and trigger actions on non-compliance.
Definition
Config records configuration states and lets you create rules to evaluate compliance against desired settings.
Example rule
s3-bucket-server-side-encryption-enabled — flags buckets without default encryption and can trigger remediation.
Design decision
Decide which rules use automatic remediation and which require human review based on risk impact.
Key Takeaway

Use Config for continuous evaluation and remediation triggers; pair it with CloudTrail for full audit context.

Evaluation & remediation pattern
Detect
Config evaluates resources against a rule and marks NON_COMPLIANT when a violation occurs.
Notify
Config can send events or SNS notifications to indicate violations and start workflows.
Remediate
Trigger a Lambda function to apply a fix such as enabling default encryption on an S3 bucket.

screens.title: Automating remediation: Config Rule + Lambda
screens.narratorSegment: Automated remediation pairs a detective control with an action that repairs the non-compliant resource. The typical flow is: AWS Config evaluates a resource and emits an event when it is NON_COMPLIANT; that event triggers a Lambda function that applies a corrective action, such as enabling default encryption on an S3 bucket. For example, the Config managed rule s3-bucket-server-side-encryption-enabled will mark an unencrypted bucket as non-compliant. A remediation Lambda receives the Config change event, extracts the bucket name, and calls the S3 A P I to put a default encryption configuration. A common misconception is that automation removes the need for auditing — automated fixes must still be logged and validated to provide evidence to auditors. When you implement this pattern, ensure the Lambda has a least-privilege role that allows s3:PutBucketEncryption and logging permissions, and test in a development account first. The visible code pane shows the Python remediation handler and an example IAM policy for the Lambda role; study them to confirm the required permissions and to understand how the event contains the resource name. After deploying, create an unencrypted bucket and observe Config marking it NON_COMPLIANT and the Lambda applying encryption. That closed-loop reduces mean time to remediation and lowers manual effort. How would you extend this pattern for a different resource type?

keyIdea.title: Remediation Pattern
keyIdea.text: Use Config rules to detect non-compliance and Lambda functions with least-privilege roles to remediate resources automatically, preserving audit evidence.

content.html:
Process Flow
Config Rule → Lambda Remediation
Detect a non-compliant resource with Config and invoke Lambda to apply a corrective action automatically.
Lambda remediation (Python)
<pre><code>import boto3 import json s3 = boto3.client('s3') def lambda_handler(event, context): # Received event from AWS Config change notification print(f"Received event: {json.dumps(event)}") invoking_event = json.loads(event['invokingEvent']) configuration_item = invoking_event['configurationItem'] bucket_name = configuration_item['resourceName'] print(f"Attempting to encrypt bucket: {bucket_name}") try: s3.put_bucket_encryption( Bucket=bucket_name, ServerSideEncryptionConfiguration={ 'Rules': [ { 'ApplyServerSideEncryptionByDefault': { 'SSEAlgorithm': 'AES256' } } ] } ) print(f"Successfully enabled default encryption for bucket: {bucket_name}") return { 'statusCode': 200, 'body': json.dumps(f"Enabled default encryption for bucket: {bucket_name}") } except Exception as e: print(f"Error encrypting bucket {bucket_name}: {e}") raise e </code></pre>
IAM role for Lambda
Lambda needs s3:PutBucketEncryption and CloudWatch Logs permissions. Use least privilege.

screens.title: AWS CloudTrail and centralized logging
screens.narratorSegment: CloudTrail provides a record of A P I calls and management events across your accounts. For large organizations, a best practice is to centralize CloudTrail logs in a dedicated logging account and protect that S3 bucket from accidental deletion, for example by applying strict bucket policies and enabling MFA Delete where required. Centralization simplifies analysis and auditing because all trails and global service events are available in one place. A concrete example is streaming CloudTrail logs to a logging account and analyzing them via Athena or a SIEM. A common mistake is leaving trails enabled only in a single region — CloudTrail should cover all regions and global service events to capture the full activity surface. For architects, ensure that logs are immutable from a business perspective and that access is tightly controlled. Also ensure that CloudTrail trails and S3 bucket policies prevent deletion by member accounts, and that access to logs is auditable. When you design logging, plan how logs will be retained to satisfy regulatory retention requirements and how you will provide auditors with evidence of controls. screens.title: Shared Responsibility Model for compliance
screens.narratorSegment: The shared responsibility model divides security responsibilities between AWS and the customer. AWS is responsible for the security of the cloud — the physical infrastructure, regions, network, and foundational services. You are responsible for security in the cloud: configuring services, managing identities, encrypting data, and operating secure workloads. When applying compliance frameworks like PCI or HIPAA, this distinction becomes operational: AWS provides certifications and controls for the infrastructure, but you must implement encryption, access controls, patching, and logging to meet specific requirements. A practical example: while AWS may provide a managed database service that is compliant with certain infrastructure controls, you still must configure encryption at rest, manage user accounts, and apply network controls. A common misconception is to assume that AWS certifications absolve you of responsibilities — they do not. For auditors, be ready to show how your architecture fulfills the customer-side controls: show IAM policies, Config rule evaluations, CloudTrail logs, and automated remediation evidence. The design implication for architects is to map each regulatory control to either an AWS responsibility or a customer responsibility and to ensure that evidence collection covers customer-implemented controls. What customer-side controls in your architecture need clearer evidence for auditors?

screens.title: Applying compliance frameworks on AWS
screens.narratorSegment: Compliance frameworks like PCI, HIPAA, GDPR, and ISO 27001 consist of controls that you must map to technical and operational measures in your AWS architecture. The practical approach is to take each control and ask two questions: which part is provided by AWS, and which part must you implement? For instance, PCI requires protecting cardholder data. AWS may provide compliant infrastructure, but you must encrypt stored data, limit access, and retain logs that show who accessed data. For GDPR, data residency and access governance are major concerns: use Organizations and SCPs to prevent resource creation in disallowed regions and enforce encryption for data at rest. For HIPAA you will need strong access controls, encryption, and auditable logs. ISO 27001 emphasizes documentation and evidence of control operation — here Config and CloudTrail become essential to demonstrate continuous compliance. A common mistake is treating certifications as a checklist that absolves you from implementing customer-side controls. Instead, architects should produce a mapping document that ties each regulatory requirement to specific AWS services, configurations, Config rules, and logging artifacts. Finally, ensure you can present evidence: Config rule evaluations, CloudTrail exports, and hardened log retention policies. Which framework would you prioritize based on your organization’s data types and geography?

screens.title: Practical governance pattern: guardrail → detect → remediate
screens.narratorSegment: A practical governance pattern combines three stages: guardrail, detect, and remediate. Guardrails are preventive: use Organizations and SCPs to block classes of risky actions, such as provisioning resources in banned regions. Detect is continuous evaluation: use AWS Config and CloudTrail to observe changes and record who did what. Remediate is corrective: use Config Rules that trigger Lambda functions to repair misconfigurations like missing encryption or public access. Concretely, the loop works like this: an SCP prevents many risky actions up front; if something slips through or is misconfigured, Config evaluates and marks the resource non-compliant; a Lambda remediation takes corrective action and writes logs; CloudTrail records the A P I calls for the investigator and the auditor. A misconception is to treat these as independent tasks; instead, design them as a closed loop with monitoring and evidence for each step. When planning the loop, prioritize high-impact rules for automatic remediation and treat higher-risk changes with manual approvals. Also ensure remediation actions themselves are auditable. This repeatable pattern scales across resource types and reduces mean time to remediation while producing clear artifacts for compliance. Which resource class would you prioritize to apply this closed-loop first?

Design a closed-loop governance workflow to prevent, detect, and correct non-compliant resources.

fullNarratorScript:
In large cloud estates, governance is not optional — it is the architecture that keeps your environment secure, auditable, and predictable. In this lesson you will learn how AWS Organizations provides the account hierarchy you need, how Service Control Policies act as preventive guardrails, and how AWS Config and CloudTrail become your continuous detective controls. You will see a concrete remediation pattern where Config rules detect a misconfigured S3 bucket and a Lambda function automatically restores encryption. Understanding the shared responsibility model is essential: AWS secures the underlying infrastructure while you must design, configure, and operate your workloads to meet compliance frameworks such as PCI, HIPAA, GDPR, and ISO 27001. Along the way we’ll point out common mistakes, like trying to use SCPs to grant permissions, or storing logs without protecting them from deletion. By the end of this chapter you’ll be able to propose a multi-account structure with OUs and SCPs, define Config rules for continuous evaluation, plan an automated remediation workflow, and explain who is responsible for each control during an audit. Consider what compliance requirement is most critical for your organization and how a combination of preventative guardrails and automated remediation would reduce manual work and risk.

Over the next screens you will develop concrete skills that let you design and operate governance at enterprise scale. First, you will design and implement a multi-account strategy using AWS Organizations and Organizational Units. This means grouping accounts to reflect teams, environments, or compliance boundaries so policies can be applied consistently. Second, you will use Service Control Policies to enforce preventative guardrails. An SCP does not grant permissions; it limits the maximum permissions available in an account or OU. A common error is attempting to use SCPs to grant access — remember they only filter permissions. Each objective includes a small mnemonic so you remember whether the control is preventative or detective. As you progress you should be able to articulate how these design choices reduce risk, prevent misconfiguration, and scale policy enforcement across many accounts. Practice applying them in a non-production environment to validate rules and avoid accidental lockouts. Consider how an OU structure in your organization would mirror business units and what operations you would block with an SCP.

In the second set of objectives you will use CloudTrail for audit trails and learn to clearly explain the shared responsibility model to auditors. CloudTrail records A P I activity and console actions so you can investigate incidents and demonstrate who did what and when. You will also learn to map compliance frameworks such as PCI, HIPAA, GDPR, and ISO 27001 to AWS controls, and to design evidence collection using Config and CloudTrail. Finally, you will practice a hands-on automation: detect unencrypted S3 buckets with a Config rule and remediate them automatically with a Lambda function. Each learning objective emphasizes why the skill matters in production: faster incident response, consistent policy enforcement, and clearer audit evidence. Keep in mind that many frameworks require both preventive and detective controls; architecture must combine both. As you study, think about how you would explain the boundary of responsibility between AWS and your organization for each control.

As a solutions architect, your responsibilities stretch beyond selecting services and writing CloudFormation. Governance is the set of patterns you design so the organization can operate securely and consistently across many accounts. That includes designing an account structure, deciding which actions are allowed or denied, choosing how logs are collected, and defining automated responses to non-compliant states. A concrete example is when an enterprise has separate accounts for finance, dev, and production: you would use Organizational Units to group accounts and apply policies tailored to risk — for instance, stricter restrictions for finance. A common misconception is that governance is only about blocking actions; in reality it balances prevention, detection, and remediation. Prevention reduces risk, but detective controls like AWS Config and CloudTrail provide evidence and help you discover gaps. For architects, the practical significance is twofold: first, policies reduce human error and accidental exposure; second, a clear governance design produces audit evidence that simplifies compliance reporting. When you design governance, think in patterns: where should a preventive guardrail be applied, what should be monitored, and what should be fixed automatically? This framing helps you justify architecture decisions to stakeholders and prepares you for audits. What part of your current account strategy would you formalize into an OU today?

AWS Organizations is the foundation for multi-account governance: it lets you consolidate accounts, centralize billing, and apply policies to groups of accounts. Organizational Units let you mirror organizational structure — for example, create OUs for engineering, finance, and production. Applying policies at the OU level is powerful because it avoids per-account replication and reduces configuration drift. A concrete example is attaching an SCP to an OU that denies launching instances in disallowed regions. Remember that SCPs define the maximum available permissions; they do not grant access. A frequent mistake is relying solely on an OU without thinking through exceptions — some accounts may require special allowances. To test safely, create a sandbox OU and a test account before applying broad SCPs. Operationally, you should also plan a logging account where CloudTrail and aggregated logs are stored, and a security account for centralized alerting. The practical insight for architects is to design OUs and SCPs so they enforce business rules while minimizing legitimate operational friction. How would you represent your organization in OUs to simplify policy application? AWS Organizations and Organizational Units means use organizations and ous to group accounts, apply policies at scale, and centralize billing and logging for consistent governance and auditability.. In practical terms, structure accounts so policies and billing are manageable at scale. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Service Control Policies are a central mechanism to set preventive guardrails across accounts. An SCP filters the maximum permissions an account or OU can exercise; it does not grant permissions by itself. For example, an SCP attached to an OU could deny the ability to create resources in a specific region or denying deletion of audit trails. A practical contrast helps: IAM policies grant or deny for a specific user or role, whereas SCPs restrict everything in an account regardless of those IAM policies, subject to the effective permission intersection. A common mistake is attempting to use an SCP as an IAM policy — because SCPs cannot grant access, an overly restrictive SCP can accidentally block administrators. To avoid that, test policies in a sandbox and use Allow-lists carefully. Another misconception is that SCPs replace logging or remediation: they prevent many misconfigurations, but you still need detective controls like Config and CloudTrail to record what did happen. The key outcome is this: use SCPs to enforce enterprise policy boundaries and prevent entire classes of risky actions, while leaving day-to-day access control to IAM within those bounds. How would you craft an SCP to prevent data storage in a disallowed region while permitting normal operations elsewhere?

SCPs are powerful, and power invites mistakes if you move too quickly. A frequent pitfall is creating a deny that inadvertently prevents critical management actions, such as updating CloudTrail configurations or applying patching tasks. Another mistake is assuming that an SCP will provide audit logs — SCPs prevent actions; they do not record them. To mitigate risk, adopt a safe testing pattern: first apply the SCP to a sandbox OU or a single test account, then simulate common administrative workflows to ensure no legitimate tasks are blocked. Use explicit denies sparingly and prefer targeted statements that address a specific risk, such as denying resource creation in a banned region. Also plan exception processes for accounts that must break the pattern, documented and approved. A practical test you can run is attempting to create a resource that the SCP would deny and confirming the expected failure message, then checking CloudTrail to confirm the attempted A P I call was recorded. The final takeaway is to treat SCP changes like schema changes: version them, review them, and deploy them progressively. What verification steps would you add to your change process to ensure an SCP doesn't block an essential operation?

AWS Config provides a continuous inventory of your resource configurations and records changes over time. It lets you define Config Rules that evaluate whether resources meet your desired conditions — for example, requiring S3 buckets to have default encryption or ensuring EC2 instances have specific tags. When a rule marks a resource NON_COMPLIANT, Config can emit notifications and trigger remediation workflows. A concrete example is the S3 default encryption rule: when an unencrypted bucket is detected, Config can publish an evaluation event that invokes a Lambda function to apply server-side encryption and return the resource to compliance. A common misconception is that Config replaces auditing practices; instead, it complements them. Config gives you continuous evaluation and point-in-time configuration history, while CloudTrail records who made A P I calls. For architects, the design decision is which rules to enforce automatically and which to surface for manual review. Automating low-risk fixes like enabling encryption reduces toil, while higher-risk changes may require human approval. When building rules, consider evaluation frequency, scope, and whether remediation should be manual or automatic. Which resource types in your environment would you automate and which would you review manually?

Automated remediation pairs a detective control with an action that repairs the non-compliant resource. The typical flow is: AWS Config evaluates a resource and emits an event when it is NON_COMPLIANT; that event triggers a Lambda function that applies a corrective action, such as enabling default encryption on an S3 bucket. For example, the Config managed rule s3-bucket-server-side-encryption-enabled will mark an unencrypted bucket as non-compliant. A remediation Lambda receives the Config change event, extracts the bucket name, and calls the S3 A P I to put a default encryption configuration. A common misconception is that automation removes the need for auditing — automated fixes must still be logged and validated to provide evidence to auditors. When you implement this pattern, ensure the Lambda has a least-privilege role that allows s3:PutBucketEncryption and logging permissions, and test in a development account first. The visible code pane shows the Python remediation handler and an example IAM policy for the Lambda role; study them to confirm the required permissions and to understand how the event contains the resource name. After deploying, create an unencrypted bucket and observe Config marking it NON_COMPLIANT and the Lambda applying encryption. That closed-loop reduces mean time to remediation and lowers manual effort. How would you extend this pattern for a different resource type?

A practical governance pattern combines three stages: guardrail, detect, and remediate. Guardrails are preventive: use Organizations and SCPs to block classes of risky actions, such as provisioning resources in banned regions. Detect is continuous evaluation: use AWS Config and CloudTrail to observe changes and record who did what. Remediate is corrective: use Config Rules that trigger Lambda functions to repair misconfigurations like missing encryption or public access. Concretely, the loop works like this: an SCP prevents many risky actions up front; if something slips through or is misconfigured, Config evaluates and marks the resource non-compliant; a Lambda remediation takes corrective action and writes logs; CloudTrail records the A P I calls for the investigator and the auditor. A misconception is to treat these as independent tasks; instead, design them as a closed loop with monitoring and evidence for each step. When planning the loop, prioritize high-impact rules for automatic remediation and treat higher-risk changes with manual approvals. Also ensure remediation actions themselves are auditable. This repeatable pattern scales across resource types and reduces mean time to remediation while producing clear artifacts for compliance.
